name: Trukese
confidence_why: Hart 1991 states outright that Trukese has no recorded stress, Goodenough and Sugita 1980 describe penultimate stress only for the earlier stage of the language before final vowels were lost, and Benton 1968 and the other works consulted give no word-stress rule, so the undetermined classification rests on few sources but meets no contrary description.
catalog_citation: Hart, Michele E. 1991. The moraic status of initial geminates in Trukese. Proceedings of the Seventeenth Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society (BLS 17), 107-120. DOI 10.3765/bls.v17i0.1635
catalog_locator: p. 108, section 1 'Background Information' and footnote 4, p. 118; saved
catalog_quote: The minimal lexical-category word in Trukese is underlyingly bimoraic: [μμ]Wmin. All monomoraic words appear to belong to functional categories, like conjunctions and complementizers, e.g: mé, 'and'; ngé, 'but, while'. Following McCarthy and Prince (1986), I assume that this bimoraic unit is also the canonical foot of the language, although there is otherwise little direct evidence for foot structure, given that there is no recorded stress.4 ... [fn. 4, p. 118] Additional evidence supporting the moraic trochee as the foot type comes from a pattern of reduplication forming denomimal verbs, which apparently maps to a suffixed bimoraic template: /waa/, 'canoe'; /waawaa/, 'use as a vehicle', but /mwaane/, 'brother'; /mwaaneane/, 'treat as a brother'.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule has been recorded for Chuukese: the phonological literature working from the standard description (Goodenough & Sugita 1980) states that there is no recorded stress, and posits a moraic-trochee foot on the basis of the bimoraic minimal word and a bimoraic reduplicative template rather than any stress facts. The only positional statement found in the primary description is historical: Goodenough & Sugita 1980 (Introduction, ca. pp. xviii-xix, seen only as archive.org search snippets) say that at the stage before final-vowel loss 'Words, including complex words, usually had a primary stress accent on the vowel of the next to last syllable, and never on the last syllable', which they use to explain the loss of final vowels; no synchronic stress rule surfaced in that volume.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Benton 1968 (p.125-126) marks 'primary sentence stress' on one example and says Eastern-lagoon dialects lengthen a stressed vowel for emphasis, i.e. prominence is treated as sentence-level.
new_statements.domain_note: Hart's statement concerns the descriptive record for the word level (foot structure); Goodenough & Sugita's penultimate statement is about a reconstructed earlier stage of the language, not modern citation forms; Benton's only stress marking is explicitly sentence stress. Data in all three are Lagoon Chuukese (Hart from Goodenough & Sugita's dictionary; Benton Eastern-lagoon dialects; Dyen's grammar, not seen, is Faichuk/western lagoon).
new_statements.first_reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Lagoon Chuukese (chuu1238): Hart 1991 uses Goodenough & Sugita's lagoon-Trukese dictionary data; Benton 1968 describes Eastern-lagoon dialects; Dyen 1965 (not seen) describes the Faichuk/western-lagoon dialect. Mortlockese (mort1237), Puluwat (pulu1242) and Saipan Carolinian (caro1242) are separate Chuukic languages and were not used for the statement; WALS's 'No fixed stress / unbounded' coding belongs to Puluwat, not Chuukese.

sources.citation: Benton, Richard A. 1968. Substitutes and classifiers in Trukese. MA thesis, University of Hawaii. 297 pp. (Glottolog grammar sketch)
sources.note: No word-stress rule. Phoneme table and remarks on vowel/consonant doubling (pp.8-9); example (128) p.125 carries the notation "' indicates primary sentence stress: vowel length"; p.126: 'in Eastern dialects emphasis is frequently indicated by lengthening a stressed vowel' and a possible 'shift in stress' explains a length alternation. Appendix p.264 notes that Dyen 1965's phonology and sandhi rules are his sections 1-65, pp.1-10, and apply to Faichuk (western lagoon) dialects.
